questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Changes in who is affected
questions.question: A digital bank's AI budgeting coach was risk-assessed for adult customers; the unchanged model will now be offered in a teen account for ages 13 to 17. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the bank keep the adult assessment, as the model is unchanged
options.B: Have the risk owner test the coach's advice on sample teen accounts
options.C: Have marketing add a parental consent screen to the new teen account
options.D: Have the risk owner reassess the coach's risks for teenage users

questions.key_concept: AI risk assessments are tied to a use and its affected people; a new user group, especially minors, triggers reassessment before launch.
questions.pre_read: Notice what changed since the original assessment, and ask whether that assessment still describes the people affected.
questions.correct_explanation: The original assessment weighed harm to adults. The model is unchanged, but teenagers differ in how they read and act on money advice, and the coach's outputs, data use and safeguards were never judged for them, so the risk owner must reassess before launch. Testing advice on teen accounts, option B, is the runner-up: it is needed, but the reassessment decides which harms and criteria the tests must cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because no model change was made. But risk depends on the use and the people affected; teenagers are a group the adult assessment never weighed.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because testing shows how the coach treats teens. But tests need criteria, and only a reassessment of harms to minors sets what to test.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because minors often need parental consent. But choosing a control before the risks are reassessed may miss harms consent cannot address.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps an assessment written for adults though the people affected have changed, and C picks a control before the risks are known.
Final two: D beats B because a new group of affected people triggers reassessment, which then sets the criteria the teen tests must use.
Exam cue: when an AI system reaches a new group of people, especially minors, expect the risk owner to reassess before launch.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Setting AI tolerances
questions.question: A legal aid charity's board states a low appetite for its eligibility-screening model wrongly rejecting people who qualify for help. Which tolerance would the IS auditor consider BEST for senior management to set within it?

options.A: At least 95% overall accuracy on the screening model's held-out test data
options.B: Caseworker review of each rejection to find applicants who qualify
options.C: No more than 1 in 100 qualifying applicants screened out each month
options.D: Monthly drift in the model's input data kept below an agreed limit

questions.key_concept: A tolerance turns appetite into a measurable limit on the harm itself; overall accuracy can stay high while that harm grows.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option could actually tell management when the board's appetite is being breached.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance sets a measurable limit, within appetite, on the harm the board named: people who qualify being wrongly rejected. A monthly cap on such rejections can be monitored and escalated. Overall accuracy, option A, is the runner-up: it is measurable, but it blends all errors, so it can stay at 95% while far more qualifying applicants are screened out.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is precise and measurable. But overall accuracy mixes all errors, so it can hold steady while qualifying applicants are wrongly rejected.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because review catches people wrongly rejected. But it is a control that reduces the harm; a tolerance is the measurable limit that control must keep it within.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because drift is a real AI risk signal. But input drift is an early warning, not a limit on the wrongful rejections the board named.

tips: Eliminate: B is a control that reduces wrongful rejections rather than a limit on them, and D tracks input drift, an early warning rather than the harm itself.
Final two: C beats A because a tolerance limits the named harm directly; overall accuracy can stay high while wrongful rejections rise.
Exam cue: a good AI tolerance measures the harm in the appetite statement, not a general model metric like accuracy.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Multi-model decisions
questions.question: An Australian immigration service runs visa applications through three models; a flag from any one sends a case toward refusal, and each meets its own wrongful-flag tolerance. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Applicants wrongly flagged may not know which model flagged them
options.B: Wrongful flags across all three models together may exceed appetite
options.C: The three models may be retrained on different schedules
options.D: Each model's tolerance may be stricter than the appetite requires

questions.key_concept: When several models feed one decision, their errors combine; tolerances must also cover the end-to-end outcome for the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Follow one applicant through every model, and ask how the chances of a wrong flag add up along the way.
questions.correct_explanation: Because a flag from any one model pushes a case toward refusal, an applicant faces three chances of a wrongful flag. Each model can meet its own tolerance while the combined rate is higher, up to the sum of all three rates, and per-model limits would never show it. Unclear sources of flags, option A, is the runner-up: it weakens appeals, but it does not show whether combined harm stays within appetite.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because applicants need to know what to appeal. But transparency helps challenge one case; it does not show whether combined wrongful flags stay within appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because retraining is a change to control. But differing schedules are a change-management detail; they do not reveal the combined error rate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because tolerances can seem meant to equal appetite. But tolerances sit within it, so stricter limits are normal and help keep combined wrongful flags in bounds.

tips: Eliminate: C is a change-management detail, and D treats tolerances set inside appetite as a flaw, though that is how tolerances work; neither shows combined wrongful flags.
Final two: B beats A because separate tolerances can each be met while combined wrongful flags exceed appetite; transparency helps appeals, not measurement.
Exam cue: when models are chained into one decision, check that someone measures the end-to-end error for the people affected, not just each model.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Vendor exit and continuity
questions.question: A veterinary diagnostics lab licenses a vendor's AI model that reads blood smears; the continuity clause escrows the model's source code if the vendor fails. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Raise the penalty the vendor pays if the model service fails
options.B: Require the vendor's annual controls report covering its data centers
options.C: Test the escrow release process with the escrow agent every year
options.D: Extend escrow to the trained model files and their configuration

questions.key_concept: Source code alone cannot rebuild a trained model; AI continuity needs the trained model files, configuration and, where possible, data.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the lab would actually need to keep reading smears if the vendor disappeared tomorrow.
questions.correct_explanation: A model's behavior lives in its trained parameters, not only in its code; rebuilding it from code would need the original training data, compute and expertise, and the result would likely still differ. Escrow must cover the trained model files and configuration. Testing the release process, option C, is the runner-up: it proves the escrow agent can release what is held, but what is held cannot run the lab's tests.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because penalties motivate vendors. But money after a failure does not keep the lab's blood tests running.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor assurance. But data center controls say nothing about whether the lab could run the model if the vendor failed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because untested escrow often fails. But a smooth release of source code alone still leaves the lab without a working trained model.

tips: Eliminate: B covers the vendor's data centers rather than continuity of the model, and A pays compensation after failure without keeping the tests running.
Final two: D beats C because testing release of source code proves nothing if code cannot rebuild the trained model the lab depends on.
Exam cue: for AI continuity, the asset to protect is the trained model and its configuration, not just the code that built it.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Vendors using other AI providers
questions.question: A Bahraini wealth manager's reporting vendor now sends client portfolio data to another firm's language model, under that firm's standard terms, to draft commentary. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important to confirm?

options.A: Whether the model provider may keep or train on client data
options.B: Whether the vendor's controls report now covers the model provider
options.C: Whether the vendor encrypts client data sent to the model provider
options.D: Whether the vendor accepts liability for the commentary's content

questions.key_concept: When a vendor passes data to another AI provider, first confirm whether that provider may retain or train on it; accountability stays with the buyer.
questions.pre_read: Trace where the client data goes next, and ask what the new party is allowed to do with it.
questions.correct_explanation: Client data now reaches a fourth party, on its standard terms, outside the original due diligence. Many model providers' standard terms let them keep inputs or use them to improve their models, which could expose confidential portfolios far beyond the original purpose. Controls-report coverage, option B, is the runner-up: it matters for assurance, but such reports cover the provider's environment, not whether its terms permit training on client data.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls reports are standard vendor assurance. But they cover operations and security, not whether the provider's terms let it keep or train on client data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because encryption protects data in transit. But it secures delivery; it does not limit what the provider may do with data once received.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because commentary errors could mislead clients. But accountability for client communications stays with the wealth manager; a liability clause cannot transfer it.

tips: Eliminate: D seeks to transfer accountability, which stays with the wealth manager, and C protects data in transit without limiting what the provider may do with it.
Final two: A beats B because the first question is what the provider may do with client data; controls reports cover its environment, not its terms of use.
Exam cue: when AI adds a party to the data flow, ask first whether that party may keep or train on the data, then how it is protected.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Data quality for training
questions.question: A bus operator will redesign routes with a demand model trained on its smartphone app's trip logs, which the data owner has checked as complete and accurate. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern?

options.A: The app's trip records used for training may not be encrypted
options.B: Riders' habits may shift once the redesigned routes begin
options.C: Riders who never use the app are absent from the training data
options.D: The quality checks were run by the data owner, not independently

questions.key_concept: Data can be complete and accurate yet unrepresentative; quality rules for training data must ask who is missing from it.
questions.pre_read: Separate how correct the records are from what the records cover, then judge each option against both.
questions.correct_explanation: Records can be complete and accurate for app users while leaving out every rider who pays cash or has no smartphone, often older or lower-income people. Routes planned from that data may serve them worse. Quality rules must cover representativeness. Independent checks, option D, are the runner-up: independence strengthens evidence, but checking completeness and accuracy again would not reveal who is missing.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because trip data needs protection. But encryption is a security control; it does not change who the training data leaves out.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because habits change with new routes. But that is a later monitoring question; the data is skewed before any route changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because owners checking their own data is weaker evidence. But an independent check of completeness and accuracy would still miss riders the app never records.

tips: Eliminate: A is a security control that leaves the data's coverage unchanged, and B is a later monitoring question, while the skew exists now.
Final two: C beats D because rechecking completeness and accuracy, however independently, cannot show riders the app never captured; representativeness is a separate test.
Exam cue: complete and accurate is not the same as representative; ask who never appears in the data the model learned from.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.3 (Scientific integrity and TEVV considerations, including data representativeness); COBIT 2019 APO14 (Managed Data)

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Reusing operational data
questions.question: A Portuguese toll-road operator's data scientists are training a model predicting each commuter's daily route from plate-camera records collected for billing, saying the model keeps no plate numbers. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the team pseudonymize plate numbers before training continues
options.B: Have the data owner decide whether billing data may train this model
options.C: Have the data owner catalog the billing records' lineage
options.D: Have IT restrict the model's training set to data scientists

questions.key_concept: Data collected for one purpose cannot be reused to train a model until its owner approves the new purpose under the collection terms.
questions.pre_read: Compare why the data was collected with what it is now being used for, and ask who can approve the difference.
questions.correct_explanation: The records were collected to bill drivers, so training a model to predict each commuter's route is a new purpose, whatever the model keeps: its predictions describe identifiable people, and models can memorize training records. The data owner must decide, with privacy advice, whether that purpose is permitted before training goes on. Recording lineage, option C, is the runner-up: it documents the data's source, but a record does not make the use permitted.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it lowers identification risk. But route patterns can still point to individuals, and pseudonymizing protects data without deciding whether the new use is allowed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because lineage is core data governance. But recording where the data came from does not decide whether training on it is allowed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because limiting access reduces exposure. But it secures the training set without deciding whether the data may be used to train this model.

tips: Eliminate: D secures the training set without settling whether it may be used, and A pseudonymizes plates, though routes still identify drivers and protecting data does not decide its use.
Final two: B beats C because lineage records the data's source but cannot approve its use; the data owner must first decide whether billing data may train this model.
Exam cue: data held for one purpose is not free to train any model, whatever the builders say the model keeps; expect the data owner to approve the new purpose first.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Customer records in prompts
questions.question: A seafood exporter's support copilot sends each customer's full account record, bank details included, to a hosted language model with every query, though most concern shipment status. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have IT encrypt traffic between the copilot and the model provider
options.B: Have the business owner pseudonymize customer names in each prompt
options.C: Have the vendor mask bank details in the copilot's answers
options.D: Have the business owner limit prompts to fields each task needs

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design for AI starts with minimization: prompts should carry only the personal data the task needs.
questions.pre_read: Follow the customer data from the copilot to the hosted model, and ask what each kind of query actually requires.
questions.correct_explanation: Every query sends bank details the hosted model never needs to answer a shipment question, so they leave the exporter's control each time. Privacy by design starts with minimization: send only the fields each task needs. Pseudonymizing names, option B, is the runner-up: it lowers identifiability, but bank details and the rest of the record still reach the provider.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects customer data. But it guards the data on the way; the provider still receives every bank detail in full.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because pseudonymizing is a privacy technique. But bank details and the rest of the record still reach the provider, though the query never needs them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because output filters are a common AI safeguard. But masking answers does nothing about the full records sent in every prompt.

tips: Eliminate: A encrypts data in transit, but the provider still receives it, and C masks answers while full records still go out in every prompt.
Final two: D beats B because sending only the fields a task needs keeps bank details from the provider; pseudonymizing names still sends them.
Exam cue: privacy by design for AI starts with the prompt; expect data minimization before filters, encryption or vendor promises.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Assessing a chatbot's privacy
questions.question: A Kenyan wildlife charity's privacy impact assessment for its donor chatbot was completed by the security team and covers only encryption and access to stored records. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the privacy officer extend it to prompts, outputs and logs
options.B: Have the vendor certify that the chatbot complies with privacy laws
options.C: Have the security team add penetration tests of the chatbot
options.D: Have the security team encrypt chat logs, prompts and stored records

questions.key_concept: A privacy impact assessment for AI covers personal data in prompts, outputs and logs, and is owned by privacy roles, not only security.
questions.pre_read: List every place donors' personal data can enter or leave the chatbot, then compare that list with what the assessment covers.
questions.correct_explanation: Donors may type personal details into the chatbot, its answers can reveal them, and chat logs keep them. A privacy impact assessment must cover purpose, consent, retention and those flows, and privacy roles own it. Encrypting chats and records, option D, is the runner-up: it notices the logs, but it treats privacy as security and still skips purpose, retention and outputs.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because certification sounds conclusive. But a vendor's claim is an input, and it cannot assess how this charity uses donors' data.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because testing finds weaknesses. But penetration tests are a security control; they do not assess how donors' personal data is used.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it extends protection to chats. But encryption guards against outsiders; it does not assess purpose, retention or what the chatbot reveals.

tips: Eliminate: C adds security testing to a privacy gap, and B relies on a vendor's claim, which cannot assess the charity's own use of donor data.
Final two: A beats D because privacy needs purpose, retention and output checks owned by privacy roles; encrypting logs is still a security answer.
Exam cue: when a privacy assessment of AI covers only security controls, expect the privacy officer to extend it to prompts, outputs and logs.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Releasing a fine-tuned model
questions.question: A funeral-services group fine-tuned a generative model on bereaved families' past emails to draft replies. Before release, which evidence would BEST show the IS auditor whether the model reveals families' personal details?

options.A: The vendor's statement that its base model protects personal details
options.B: The output filter's settings for blocking phone numbers and addresses
options.C: Results of extraction tests probing for memorized family details
options.D: Confirmation that the families' emails were deleted after fine-tuning

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuned models can memorize training text; tests that try to extract it show whether personal data could leak in outputs.
questions.pre_read: Ask where families' details could still exist after training, and which evidence actually probes that place.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning on distinctive personal text such as families' emails raises the chance the model memorizes and repeats details. Extraction tests that prompt the model to reproduce training text give the most direct evidence of whether it leaks. The output filter's settings, option B, are the runner-up: a filter helps, but settings show intent, not behavior, and pattern blocking misses names and causes of death.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor built the base model. But its statement covers the base model, not memorization from the group's own fine-tuning data.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because filters are a common output control. But settings show what was configured, not what leaks; names and causes of death match no phone-number pattern.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because deleting source data seems final. But a model keeps what it memorized during fine-tuning, so deletion says nothing about its outputs.

tips: Eliminate: D deletes the source but not what the model memorized, and A covers the vendor's base model, not the group's fine-tuning on families' emails.
Final two: C beats B because extraction tests show what the model actually reveals; filter settings show intent and miss details that fit no pattern.
Exam cue: to judge whether a generative model leaks training data, prefer tests that try to extract it over settings, deletions or vendor claims.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Erasure requests and trained models
questions.question: A podcast app's data team concluded by itself that reviews erased at users' request, a tiny share of its generative model's training data, need no model action. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the model owner order retraining after every erasure request
options.B: Have the model owner decide, with the privacy officer confirming
options.C: Have IT confirm the users' reviews were deleted from every system
options.D: Have the data team record its reasoning in the erasure log

questions.key_concept: Whether erasure requires model action is the model owner's decision, confirmed by the privacy officer; a small share of data does not rule out memorization.
questions.pre_read: Ask who should own a decision about a legal duty, and whether the reason given actually holds for generative models.
questions.correct_explanation: Generative models can memorize even data that appears in few training examples, so a tiny share is no proof the reviews are gone. Whether to retrain, filter outputs or record low risk is the model owner's decision, with the privacy officer confirming it meets the legal duty. Recording the reasoning, option D, is the runner-up: it creates a trail, but the flawed decision stays with the builders.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because retraining removes the data. But a blanket rule is costly and not always needed; each case calls for weighing retraining, output filtering or recorded low risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because complete deletion seems to answer the request. But deleting source reviews does not remove what the trained model may have memorized.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because documented decisions can be reviewed. But recording a flawed share-based argument leaves the builders deciding a legal duty without the model owner or the privacy officer.

tips: Eliminate: A sets blanket retraining for every request, though each case needs weighing, and C deletes source reviews, which does not touch what the model memorized.
Final two: B beats D because memorization can occur even for rare examples, so the decision needs the accountable model owner and the privacy officer, not the builders' recorded judgment.
Exam cue: after an erasure request, the model owner decides what happens to trained models, with the privacy officer confirming; data share alone proves nothing.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Replacing a scoring method
questions.question: A Moroccan development agency replaced its points-based grant scoring with a model 6% more accurate at predicting business survival; rejected applicants are entitled to reasons. Which question should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Whether the model can explain each decision in terms people understand
options.B: Whether the agency's systems can score applicants as fast as before
options.C: Whether the model's 6% gain held on data kept back from builders
options.D: Whether reasons given under the old points rules were archived

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI characteristics trade off; a gain in accuracy cannot override an explainability requirement owed to the people affected.
questions.pre_read: Read the stem for any duty owed to the people affected, then test each option against it.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST notes that accuracy and interpretability can trade off. Here the agency owes every rejected applicant reasons, so a more accurate model that cannot produce meaningful ones fails a requirement, whatever its gain. Confirming the 6% on unseen data, option C, is the runner-up: it tests whether the gain is real, but a real gain still would not meet the duty to explain.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complex models need capacity. But speed is an operational question; it does not affect what the agency owes rejected applicants.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because claimed gains need independent proof. But even a confirmed 6% gain would not let the agency give rejected applicants the reasons they are owed.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because records support later review. But archiving past reasons concerns old decisions; it does not show the new model can explain new ones.

tips: Eliminate: B is an operational speed question, and D archives reasons for past decisions; neither shows the new model can explain its rejections.
Final two: A beats C because a confirmed accuracy gain still cannot meet the duty to give reasons; explainability here is a requirement, not a preference.
Exam cue: when a more accurate model replaces an explainable one, check first whether the people affected can still get the explanations they are owed.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Criteria for AI principles
questions.question: An Estonian ferry operator's AI principles say its booking chatbot must be transparent. Which owner-set criterion would BEST let the IS auditor test that principle?

options.A: The vendor publishes an annual transparency report on its model
options.B: Chatbot fare answers match the published fare table in 99% of tests
options.C: The chatbot is designed to be open and honest with passengers
options.D: Every chat starts by telling passengers they are talking to AI

questions.key_concept: A principle becomes auditable when owners state it as an observable criterion that measures that principle in this use, such as disclosure in every chat.
questions.pre_read: For each option, ask whether a tester could check it in this chatbot, and which trustworthy-AI quality it would actually measure.
questions.correct_explanation: Transparency in the NIST framework concerns what information about an AI system is available to the people interacting with it. A rule that every chat opens by saying the passenger is talking to AI is specific to this use and can be checked chat by chat. Fare accuracy, option B, is the runner-up: it is testable, but it measures validity, not transparency.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is published and independent of the operator. But it describes the vendor's model in general, not what passengers are told in this chatbot.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it is specific and testable. But matching fares tests whether answers are valid, not whether passengers know they are dealing with AI.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because it sounds like the principle. But a design aim restates the principle; it gives a tester nothing measurable to check.

tips: Eliminate: C restates the principle without anything to measure, and A is the vendor's general report, which cannot be checked against this chatbot.
Final two: D beats B because transparency concerns what people are told about the AI; fare accuracy is testable but measures validity, a different characteristic.
Exam cue: a testable criterion must also measure the right characteristic; ask which trustworthy-AI quality each option actually tests.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Uses outside a law's scope
questions.question: Legal counsel finds a supermarket chain's pricing model outside a new AI law, so the AI governance committee proposes dropping checks for unfair prices in low-income areas. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Replace the checks by removing income data from the model's inputs
options.B: Drop the checks, since the law defines what shoppers are owed
options.C: Keep the checks as part of managing the model's risk to shoppers
options.D: Have counsel recheck the law's scope at each annual compliance review

questions.key_concept: Legal compliance is a floor: an AI use outside one law still answers to other laws, the organization's principles and its risk appetite.
questions.pre_read: Ask what besides this one law should govern how the model treats shoppers.
questions.correct_explanation: Being outside one AI law removes that law's duties, not the risk that the model charges low-income neighborhoods more, which other laws and the chain's own risk management may still need to address. Removing income data, option A, is the runner-up: it looks like a fix, but store location and other inputs can stand in for income, so only outcome checks reveal unfair prices.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because removing income data seems to remove the bias. But store location and other inputs can stand in for income, so only outcome checks show unfair prices.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because counsel has confirmed scope. But one law is a floor; other laws and the chain's own risk limits still apply to unfair pricing.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because laws change and scope can shift. But rechecking scope still treats one law as the only reason to test for unfair prices.

tips: Eliminate: B treats one law as the whole standard, though it is only a floor, and D keeps tracking legal scope while the pricing harm goes unchecked.
Final two: C beats A because other inputs, such as store location, can stand in for income; only checking actual prices shows whether low-income areas pay more.
Exam cue: being outside one AI law does not end the duty to manage harm; expect checks to follow risk to people, not just legal scope.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Deciding which laws apply
questions.question: A cosmetics retailer's app uses a vendor's skin-analysis model, and the vendor says a new AI law's high-risk rules do not apply. Who should the IS auditor expect to hold PRIMARY responsibility for that judgment?

options.A: The retailer's AI governance committee, voting on the vendor's view
options.B: The retailer's legal counsel, advised by the model owner
options.C: The IS auditor, after testing the model's controls in the app
options.D: The vendor, which built the model and knows its design best

questions.key_concept: Whether an AI law's duties apply to the organization depends on its own use and market; that is a legal judgment for its counsel.
questions.pre_read: Separate who built the model from who uses it, and ask who should judge what the law requires of the retailer.
questions.correct_explanation: Applicability turns on how, where and for whom the retailer uses the model, which the retailer knows best, so it is a legal judgment for the retailer's counsel, informed by the model owner's description of the use. The AI governance committee, option A, is the runner-up: it approves high-impact uses and acts on the answer, but a vote cannot replace a legal judgment.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the committee governs AI uses. But applicability is a legal judgment; the committee acts on counsel's answer rather than voting on a vendor's view.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because IS auditors assess compliance. But applicability is a legal judgment for counsel; the IS auditor later tests the mapping and evidence rather than deciding applicability.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the vendor knows the model's design. But the retailer's own duties depend on its use, so the vendor's view is an input to counsel, not the judgment.

tips: Eliminate: D leaves applicability to the vendor, whose view is only an input, and C has the IS auditor making a judgment it must later assess.
Final two: B beats A because applicability is a legal judgment about the retailer's own use; the committee acts on that answer rather than replacing it.
Exam cue: who decides whether an AI law applies? Legal counsel, using the owner's account of the use; vendors advise and IS auditors test.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. A certified AI management system
questions.question: A dental-supplies distributor holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its AI management system, and its board asks whether the NIST AI RMF adds anything for its clinic credit-limit model. What is the IS auditor's BEST answer?

options.A: It repeats what the certificate already shows about model risk
options.B: It is a US legal duty the certificate does not yet meet
options.C: It is written for generative AI rather than credit-limit models
options.D: It guides mapping and measuring this model's own risks

questions.key_concept: A management-system certificate covers the process within its scope; the voluntary, use-case-agnostic NIST AI RMF can still guide model-level risk work.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the certificate's auditors actually examined, then compare that with what each option claims about the NIST framework.
questions.correct_explanation: Certification shows the distributor's AI management system meets ISO/IEC 42001 within its scope; it does not test how this model behaves. The NIST AI RMF, voluntary and use-case agnostic, adds detailed Map and Measure guidance at model level: context, affected clinics, tolerances and testing. That the certificate already covers model risk, option A, is the runner-up: it is a common reading, but certification covers the management system, not the model.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because certification involves independent auditors. But they assess the management system within its scope, not how this credit-limit model treats clinics.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because NIST is a US government body. But NIST describes the AI RMF as voluntary; it guides risk work and creates no legal duty.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because NIST also publishes a generative AI profile. But the AI RMF itself is use-case agnostic and covers predictive models like this one.

tips: Eliminate: B treats the voluntary NIST framework as a legal duty, and C limits it to generative AI, though the framework is use-case agnostic.
Final two: D beats A because a management-system certificate shows how AI is governed within its scope, not how well this model's risks were mapped and measured.
Exam cue: frameworks and certificates combine; a certified management system still needs model-level risk work, which the NIST functions can guide.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Applying the NIST AI RMF
questions.question: A ship classification society using the NIST AI RMF has tested its inspection-scheduling model for bias and robustness, but never documented its intended use, affected parties or tolerances. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the model owner define the context of use before more testing
options.B: Have the model owner choose responses to the issues tests found
options.C: Have the society seek external certification of its AI management system
options.D: Have the team extend robustness testing to more attack types

questions.key_concept: In the NIST AI RMF, Map outcomes such as intended use, affected parties and tolerances are the basis for judging Measure results and Manage responses.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a tester needs to know before deciding whether a bias or robustness result is good enough.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST describes Map outcomes as the basis for Measure and Manage: without a documented intended use, affected parties and tolerances, nobody can say which test results matter or what level is acceptable. The model owner should document that context first, with tolerances from senior management. Choosing risk responses, option B, is the runner-up: acting on findings seems decisive, but responses chosen without tolerances have nothing to aim at.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because findings call for action. But without tolerances and intended use, there is no basis for deciding which findings need a response or how much.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because certification sounds like assurance. But a management-system certificate covers process scope; it does not supply this model's missing context.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because broader testing finds more issues. But more tests without context produce more results nobody can judge against a purpose or tolerance.

tips: Eliminate: D adds tests that still lack a basis for judgment, and C seeks a process certificate, which cannot supply the model's missing context.
Final two: A beats B because responses need tolerances to aim at; Map outcomes are the basis for both Measure and Manage.
Exam cue: in the NIST AI RMF, expect context (intended use, affected people, tolerances) to be set before test results or responses are judged.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Chatbots gaining new functions
questions.question: A Uruguayan sports federation's member chatbot, inventoried as a low-risk question-answering tool, can now cancel athlete registrations and waive license fees through federation systems. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the owner require staff approval for fee waivers above a limit
options.B: Have the owner retrain the chatbot to refuse risky requests
options.C: Have the owner reclassify it as agentic and reassess its risk tier
options.D: Have IT security test the chatbot's links to federation systems

questions.key_concept: An AI system that calls tools to change records is agentic; its classification and risk tier, not its underlying model, decide the controls it needs.
questions.pre_read: Note what the system can now do, compared with what its inventory entry assumes, before judging any single control.
questions.correct_explanation: Once the chatbot can cancel registrations and waive fees, it is agentic: it acts in federation systems instead of only answering. Its tier was set for a question-answering tool, so the owner must reclassify it and reassess its risk, which then decides the limits, approvals and oversight it needs. Approval for large fee waivers, option A, is the runner-up: it is a sound control, but it covers one action and leaves cancellations unchecked.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approval limits suit agentic AI. But one limit on fee waivers leaves registration cancellations unchecked; the reassessed tier should decide which limits and approvals apply.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a better-trained model errs less. But training cannot guarantee refusals; the reassessed tier must first decide which limits outside the model the chatbot needs.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because new system connections raise security risk. But security testing shows whether the links can be attacked, not what the chatbot may decide to do through them.

tips: Eliminate: B relies on retraining, which cannot guarantee refusals, and D tests security, which says nothing about what the chatbot decides to change.
Final two: C beats A because the reassessed tier decides which limits and approvals apply; one approval rule covers fee waivers but leaves registration cancellations unchecked.
Exam cue: when an AI system gains the ability to act, reclassify it and reassess its risk before choosing individual controls.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Grounded generative answers
questions.question: A Bhutanese trekking operator's booking chatbot retrieves passages from its current permit and refund terms before generating each answer, so managers say its answers are facts. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: Running costs may rise as more travelers use the chatbot
options.B: Replies may misstate or merge the terms retrieved for them
options.C: Staff may edit the refund terms without change approval
options.D: Travelers may enter passport details that the chat log then keeps

questions.key_concept: Retrieval grounds generative answers in sources, but the model still writes the text and can misstate them, so answers still need checking.
questions.pre_read: Ask which part of the system writes the final answer, and whether that part can still get things wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Retrieval grounds the chatbot in current terms, but a generative model still writes each answer, and it can misstate, drop or merge what it retrieved while sounding certain. Treating answers as facts removes the check that would catch this. Option C, unapproved edits to the terms, is the runner-up: source integrity matters, but the stem gives no sign of it, while the managers' belief points straight at unverified answers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because running costs grow with use. But higher costs do not make answers wrong, and the managers' claim concerns whether answers are facts.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a chatbot is only as good as its sources. But nothing suggests the terms are edited without approval; the stated belief concerns how far answers can be trusted.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because chat logs can hold personal data. But that concerns what travelers type in, not whether the chatbot's answers can be trusted as facts.

tips: Eliminate: A is a cost issue that does not make answers wrong, and D concerns what travelers type in, not whether the answers can be trusted.
Final two: B beats C because a grounded model still generates its answers and can misstate sources; edits to the terms are a real risk the stem never points to.
Exam cue: retrieval reduces confabulation but does not remove it; generated answers stay unverified until checked against their sources.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 600-1 Section 2.2 (Confabulation); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 2.2 (Knowledge limits and human oversight of outputs documented)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Unsupervised groupings
questions.question: An Indian state's building-permit office uses a model that groups applications into clusters without labeled outcomes; staff named one cluster 'high fraud risk'. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: The model cannot explain why each application joined its cluster
options.B: The named cluster may shift between runs on new applications
options.C: The model's settings and number of clusters were not documented
options.D: Nothing shows the named cluster holds more fraud than the others

questions.key_concept: Unsupervised models group similar records without learning outcomes; any name given to a cluster is a hypothesis to test against confirmed cases.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model learned from, and where the cluster's name came from.
questions.correct_explanation: A clustering model finds groups of similar applications but learns no outcome, so a cluster has no meaning until people give it one. Calling a cluster 'high fraud risk' is a hypothesis; until it is checked against confirmed fraud cases, applicants could face checks on a label nobody tested. Unstable clusters, option B, is the runner-up: stability matters, but a stable cluster can still hold no more fraud than any other.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because applicants checked on a model's output deserve reasons. But explaining why an application joined a cluster would not show that the cluster holds more fraud.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because clusters can change between runs. But a perfectly stable cluster could still hold no more fraud than others; the name itself is untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because undocumented settings hinder review. But documenting them would not show whether the named cluster really holds more fraud.

tips: Eliminate: A explains cluster membership and C documents settings; neither shows whether the named cluster really holds more fraud.
Final two: D beats B because a stable cluster can still hold no extra fraud; the name staff gave it is untested until checked against confirmed cases.
Exam cue: a cluster from an unsupervised model means only what people say it means; check the label against real outcomes before it drives decisions.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Features and validation results
questions.question: A Thai motor insurer's claim-fraud model, which scores claims at intake, reached 98% validation accuracy; its strongest feature records whether investigators later opened a case. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: The feature is not yet known when the model makes each prediction
options.B: The 98% may fall slowly as fraud patterns drift over time
options.C: The validation set may be too small to support a 98% figure
options.D: The feature may carry investigators' bias against some groups of drivers

questions.key_concept: A feature recorded after the outcome leaks the answer into validation; the model scores high in testing but meets real claims without that clue.
questions.pre_read: Compare when the model makes its prediction with when each feature it uses becomes known.
questions.correct_explanation: The model was validated with a feature that records what happened after intake, a form of target leakage: at intake, no investigator has opened a case yet. The 98% is inflated, and real claims will be scored without that clue, at an accuracy nobody measured. Investigator bias, option D, is the runner-up: it is a real fairness concern, but the leaked feature makes the whole validation result unreliable first.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because fraud patterns do change. But drift develops after launch; here the feature is missing from the first day, so the 98% never applied to live claims.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because small samples give unstable figures. But a larger validation set would still contain the leaked feature, so the figure would stay inflated.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because investigators' choices can carry bias. But the larger flaw comes first: the feature does not exist at intake, so the 98% says little about the deployed model.

tips: Eliminate: B treats the problem as slow drift, though the feature is missing from day one, and C questions sample size, which cannot fix a feature that leaks the outcome.
Final two: A beats D because a feature unknown when the model predicts makes the 98% meaningless for every claim; investigator bias is a real but narrower concern.
Exam cue: check that every feature a model uses exists at the moment it predicts; if not, validation results are inflated.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.3 (Performance measured in conditions similar to deployment); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.5 (System shown to be valid and reliable, limits documented)

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Sourcing against requirements
questions.question: A Namibian fisheries ministry requires each vessel's inspection priority to be explainable to the vessel's operator, but its preferred hosted model, not yet contracted, returns only a score. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have the vendor promise to add score explanations to its service
options.B: Have the owner weigh other sourcing options against the requirement
options.C: Have inspectors write their own reasons for each vessel's priority score
options.D: Waive the requirement, since most hosted models give scores alone

questions.key_concept: Sourcing follows requirements: build, buy, fine-tune and hosted options are judged against stated needs, such as explainability, before one is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Check each option against the stated requirement, and ask whether it changes the technology or the requirement.
questions.correct_explanation: The explanation requirement is a condition the sourcing choice must meet, and a hosted model that returns a bare score does not meet it as offered. With no contract signed, the owner should first weigh other options, such as an interpretable model or a service that explains each score. A vendor promise, option A, is the runner-up: it may help later, but a promised feature is not evidence the requirement will be met.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor could close the gap. But a promise of a future feature is not evidence the requirement will be met when vessels are prioritized.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because people can explain decisions. But reasons written afterwards may not reflect what drove the model's score, so vessel operators would get explanations that are not the model's.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it lets the project proceed. But requirements come before technology; dropping one to fit a preferred model reverses the order.

tips: Eliminate: D drops a requirement to fit the technology, and C has inspectors supply reasons that may not reflect what drove the model's score.
Final two: B beats A because sourcing must follow the requirement; a vendor's promise of future explanations is not evidence the chosen model can meet it.
Exam cue: when a preferred model cannot meet a stated requirement, revisit the sourcing choice; never bend the requirement to the model.

questions.subtopic: 1A AI models and requirements. Fine-tuning a language model
questions.question: A Ghanaian pharmacy regulator will fine-tune a language model once on its approved-medicines list, which changes weekly, to answer pharmacists' approval queries. Which concern should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Pharmacists may not be told a language model writes the answers
options.B: The model may invent medicine names that the list does not contain
options.C: Answers would reflect the list as it stood when fine-tuning ended
options.D: Fine-tuning and hosting may cost more than the business case assumed

questions.key_concept: Fine-tuning fixes what a model knows at training time; a requirement for current answers needs a design that reads a maintained source.
questions.pre_read: Compare how often the source content changes with when the model learns it.
questions.correct_explanation: Fine-tuning fixes what a model learned at training time; it does not look anything up later. A list that changes weekly would be out of date within days, so answers about newly approved or withdrawn medicines would be wrong while sounding certain. Invented medicine names, option B, is the runner-up: confabulation is a real risk, but the stem's deciding fact is a weekly-changing list learned once.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because disclosure is good practice. But telling pharmacists that a model answers does not make its answers current or correct.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because language models can confabulate. But the stem's deciding fact is a list that changes weekly and is learned once, so stale answers are certain, not just possible.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because AI projects often overrun budgets. But cost does not affect whether pharmacists get correct answers about approved medicines.

tips: Eliminate: D is a budget question that does not affect answer quality, and A concerns disclosure to pharmacists, not whether the answers are correct.
Final two: C beats B because a list learned once goes out of date within a week; confabulation is real, but the stated fact points to stale knowledge.
Exam cue: fine-tuning bakes knowledge in at training time; content that changes often needs retrieval from a maintained source, not a one-time tune.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Testing inventory completeness
questions.question: A Kuwaiti petrochemical company's AI inventory lists the AI products department heads said they bought, though its engineers also build their own models. Which source would BEST help the IS auditor find missing AI?

options.A: The IT asset register of approved hardware and software products
options.B: Department heads' signed statements that their survey answers are complete
options.C: The AI governance committee's minutes approving each model before use
options.D: Job logs from the cloud platform used for model training

questions.key_concept: AI inventories built from purchase surveys miss models built in-house; completeness is tested against sources such as training platform logs, not self-reports.
questions.pre_read: Ask how AI can enter the organization without anyone buying an AI product, then find a source that would show it.
questions.correct_explanation: A survey of purchases cannot see models that engineers build themselves, since nobody buys them as products. Job logs from the cloud platform used for training show which models were actually trained and run, an independent source for that blind spot. The IT asset register, option A, is the runner-up: it is independent of the survey, but it lists bought hardware and software, not models built in-house.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it is an independent, complete list of software. But it records products the company acquired, not models its own engineers built and trained.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because signed confirmations add accountability. But the same department heads would confirm the same answers; they cannot report AI they do not know about.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because minutes are formal records. But they list only models that went through approval, so they cannot reveal models that bypassed it.

tips: Eliminate: B asks the same department heads to confirm their own answers, and C lists approved models, so it cannot reveal models that bypassed approval.
Final two: D beats A because in-house models are never bought; the asset register lists acquired products, while training job logs show what engineers actually built.
Exam cue: test AI inventory completeness against sources that show how AI really arrives, such as platform logs, vendor updates, network traffic and spending.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Risk tiers and human approval
questions.question: An Ivorian cocoa trader's AI policy rates any use low risk if a person approves each output, including a model ranking warehouse staff for redundancy. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the low tier, since a person makes each final redundancy decision
options.B: Have the policy owner drop the rule that approval lowers the tier
options.C: Have managers record a reason for each ranking they approve
options.D: Have IT review the ranking model's access controls and hosting

questions.key_concept: Tier AI uses by inherent risk, before controls; a human approval step is a control to judge, not a reason to lower a tier.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the person approving each output changes how much harm a wrong ranking could do.
questions.correct_explanation: A person approving each output does not make a use low risk: a wrong ranking can still cost staff their jobs, and approvers may simply accept what the model shows. Tiers follow each use's inherent risk, before any approval step, so the policy owner should drop the rule that approval lowers a tier. Option C, recorded reasons, is the runner-up: it may help review this model, but the rule still under-rates every approved use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a person signs each decision. But approval does not reduce the harm of a wrong ranking, and approvers often accept what the model shows.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because written reasons discourage rubber-stamping. But it treats one model, while the policy rule keeps rating every use with an approval step as low risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because staff data needs protection. But access and hosting reviews are security checks; they do not correct a tier that ignores impact.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes a person's approval lowers the impact of a wrong ranking, and D reviews security, which does not correct how the use was tiered.
Final two: B beats C because the tiering rule under-rates every use with an approval step; recorded reasons may help this model but leave the rule in place.
Exam cue: a human approval step does not make an AI use low risk; tier each use by inherent risk, then judge the approval as a control.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Committee membership
questions.question: A Mozambican ministry's AI governance committee (two IT managers, one data science lead) approved a model ranking patients for scarce dialysis places; the lead, its builder, abstained. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: No one accountable for dialysis allocation took part in approving it
options.B: The committee may meet too rarely to approve dialysis models quickly
options.C: The IT managers may lack training in machine-learning methods
options.D: No IS auditor sat on the committee as a voting member

questions.key_concept: High-impact AI uses need approval by people accountable for the decision and its legal duties, not only those who build and run the model.
questions.pre_read: List who sits on the committee, then ask who answers if a patient is wrongly ranked down the list.
questions.correct_explanation: Ranking patients for scarce dialysis is a clinical, legal and ethical decision with direct harm to people, so the approving committee needs the clinical owner and the legal and ethics functions that answer for that harm. With the builder abstaining, only IT approved, and IT judges technical fitness, not whether delayed treatment is acceptable. Machine-learning training, option C, is the runner-up: it would sharpen technical review but add nobody accountable for allocation.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because slow approvals frustrate projects. But meeting more often would not give the committee the people who answer for dialysis allocation.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI seems to need technical approvers. But more machine-learning skill would still leave nobody who answers for dialysis allocation approving the model.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because audit brings independence. But a voting IS auditor would be approving an AI use that audit must later assess; audit may advise, never approve.

tips: Eliminate: B is about meeting speed, which does not make approvals sound, and D would have the IS auditor approve an AI use that audit must later assess.
Final two: A beats C because technical training adds nobody who answers for dialysis allocation; the committee lacks the owners of the harm, not machine-learning skill.
Exam cue: AI risk is not an IT or data science matter alone; expect those who own the decision and its legal duties to approve high-impact uses.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Agents across departments
questions.question: A Panamanian shipping agency's AI agent books port services, pays invoices and updates crew rosters in three departments' systems; its inventory entry names no owner. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The agent's language model may word supplier messages inconsistently
options.B: Each system may log the agent's actions in a different format
options.C: System owners may grant the agent more access than its tasks need
options.D: No one has authority to limit or stop the agent across systems

questions.key_concept: An AI agent acting across several systems needs one named owner with authority over its combined actions; each system owner sees only part.
questions.pre_read: Picture the agent making one wrong booking, payment and roster change; ask who could stop it.
questions.correct_explanation: Each department owns one system, but the agent acts across all three, so its combined behavior, such as booking a service, paying for it and changing crews, belongs to no one. Without a named owner, nobody sets its limits, accepts its risks or can stop it. Excess access, option C, is the runner-up: least privilege matters, but each system owner sees only one slice, so no one judges the agent's total power.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because generated messages can vary. But inconsistent wording causes little harm compared with unowned payments and roster changes.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because scattered logs slow investigations. But better logs record what the agent did; they give nobody authority to limit or stop it.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because agents often hold excess access. But each system owner grants access for one slice; without an agent owner, nobody judges its total power.

tips: Eliminate: A is a wording issue with little harm, and B improves records of the agent's actions without giving anyone authority over them.
Final two: D beats C because access granted system by system leaves the agent's combined actions unowned; someone must answer for them and be able to stop it.
Exam cue: an AI agent that acts across systems needs its own named owner with authority to limit and stop it, beyond each system's owner.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Program metrics for the board
questions.question: A Qatari investment group's quarterly AI program report to its board shows models deployed and AI spending against budget. Which added metric should the IS auditor recommend as BEST evidence that AI governance works?

options.A: Average accuracy of deployed models at their latest validation
options.B: Average monthly response time of the group's AI services
options.C: Share of high-impact models overdue for scheduled validation
options.D: Number of new AI use cases that business units proposed

questions.key_concept: AI program metrics show whether governance operates, such as overdue validations of high-impact models, not adoption, spending or average model accuracy.
questions.pre_read: For each metric, ask whether it could look good while the riskiest models go unchecked.
questions.correct_explanation: Governance works when its controls operate: models have owners, and risk reviews and validations happen on schedule. The share of high-impact models overdue for validation shows directly whether the program keeps its riskiest AI under review. Average accuracy at the latest validation, option A, is the runner-up: it sounds like assurance, but an average can look good while the riskiest models go unvalidated, and accuracy measures models, not governance.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because accuracy sounds like assurance. But an average across models can look good while high-impact models sit unvalidated; it measures models, not whether governance controls operate.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because service speed matters to users. But response time is a performance measure, not evidence that governance controls operate.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it shows the program's reach. But proposals count adoption, which can grow whether or not AI is governed.

tips: Eliminate: D counts adoption, which grows whether or not AI is governed, and B measures service speed, a performance metric.
Final two: C beats A because overdue validations show whether controls over the riskiest models operate; an average accuracy can look good while those models go unchecked.
Exam cue: AI program metrics should show whether governance controls operate, such as overdue reviews, missing owners and incidents.

questions.subtopic: 1B AI governance. Measuring AI-assisted work
questions.question: A Serbian gas utility reports, as its AI program's main success measure, that 96% of AI-drafted replies to billing disputes are sent without edits. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: A high no-edit rate may reflect unchecked drafts, not good ones
options.B: Customers may not know that a model drafted their replies
options.C: Reviewers' edits may not be logged reliably for every reply
options.D: The measure leaves out the staff hours the drafts save

questions.key_concept: A high rate of AI output accepted unchanged can signal automation bias; program metrics need direct quality checks, not acceptance rates.
questions.pre_read: Ask what else, besides good drafts, could make reviewers send most replies unchanged.
questions.correct_explanation: A reply sent unedited may mean the draft was right, or that reviewers stopped checking: automation bias looks the same in this metric. Treating the rate as success rewards rubber-stamping, so the program needs a direct measure of quality, such as sampled replies checked for errors. Unreliable edit logging, option C, is the runner-up: data quality matters, but even perfectly logged, the rate cannot tell good drafts from unchecked ones.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because disclosure matters for trust. But it does not change what the success measure shows about the quality of replies.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because a metric is only as good as its data. But even perfectly logged, a no-edit rate cannot separate correct drafts from drafts nobody checked.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because programs should show value. But adding hours saved measures efficiency; it says nothing about whether the replies are right.

tips: Eliminate: D asks for an efficiency measure, which says nothing about quality, and B concerns disclosure to customers, not what the success measure shows.
Final two: A beats C because even perfectly recorded, a no-edit rate cannot separate correct drafts from unchecked ones; the measure itself is the problem.
Exam cue: treat high acceptance of AI output as a possible sign of automation bias until sampled quality checks show the output is right.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Basis for accepting AI risk
questions.question: An Egyptian licensing board's exam face-verification model wrongly rejects candidates aged over 60 three times as often as others; the risk owner accepted it, citing 97% overall accuracy. What is the IS auditor's BEST action?

options.A: Reperform the 97% accuracy figure on recent check-in records
options.B: Report that the acceptance did not weigh harm to older candidates
options.C: Overturn the acceptance and suspend checks for older candidates
options.D: Leave the acceptance alone, since accepting risk is management's call

questions.key_concept: Risk owners choose the response, but an acceptance resting on overall accuracy that ignores harm to one group is uninformed and reportable.
questions.pre_read: Separate who decides the risk response from what the IS auditor checks about that decision.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk acceptance is the owner's call, but the IS auditor assesses whether it was informed. The 97% overall figure hides that candidates aged over 60 are wrongly turned away three times as often, a harm the acceptance never weighed, so the IS auditor reports it for the owner to reconsider. Reperforming the 97%, option A, is the runner-up: it checks the figure, but a correct overall figure would still hide the harm to older candidates.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reperformance is strong audit evidence. But a confirmed overall figure would still average away the higher error rate for candidates aged over 60.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the harm is clear. But overturning a risk acceptance or suspending the model is the owner's decision; the IS auditor reports and recommends.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because risk acceptance belongs to management. But the IS auditor still assesses whether the acceptance was informed and reports when it was not.

tips: Eliminate: C has the IS auditor overturning a decision that belongs to the owner, and D treats management's right to accept risk as putting its basis beyond audit.
Final two: B beats A because a correct overall figure would still hide the harm to older candidates; the gap is what the acceptance weighed, not the figure's accuracy.
Exam cue: an AI risk acceptance resting on one overall score is uninformed if one group bears more errors; report it and let the owner decide again.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Rating rare AI errors
questions.question: A Swiss canton's model translates flood warnings into eight languages; its risk register rates the risk low on error frequency alone, citing 99.5% benchmark accuracy. Which question should the IS auditor raise as MOST important?

options.A: Whether the translation vendor holds a current security certification
options.B: Whether the 99.5% was measured on the model version now in use
options.C: Whether residents are told that a model translated the warnings
options.D: Whether the harm one wrong warning could cause was weighed

questions.key_concept: AI risk ratings combine likelihood and impact on people; a rare error can still make a high risk when its consequence is severe.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the rating left out, and what one wrong flood warning would mean for a resident.
questions.correct_explanation: Benchmark accuracy speaks only to how often errors occur, which is half of a rating. A machine-translated warning often reads fluently even when wrong, so residents have no reason to doubt it, and one wrong flood instruction can cost lives. The rating must weigh that impact on people too. Whether the 99.5% reflects the model version in use, option B, is the runner-up: it firms up likelihood but leaves impact unweighed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because vendors handle the translations. But security certification says nothing about how severe a mistranslated warning would be.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a model update can change its accuracy. But a current figure only firms up likelihood; the rating would still ignore what one wrong warning could cost residents.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because disclosure supports trust. But telling residents a model translated the warning does not change how harmful a wrong instruction could be.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the risk as a security question and C concerns disclosure; neither affects how severe a mistranslated warning could be.
Final two: D beats B because benchmark accuracy speaks to likelihood alone; tying it to the current model version still leaves the harm of one wrong warning unweighed.
Exam cue: an AI risk rated low on high accuracy is incomplete; fluent AI errors go unnoticed, so rate likelihood and impact on the people affected together.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Indicators for refund holds
questions.question: A Tanzanian revenue authority's model holds suspected fraudulent VAT refunds; wrongful holds surface only after two-month reviews. Which key risk indicator (KRI) should the IS auditor recommend as BEST early warning of a tolerance breach?

options.A: Monthly value of fraud losses that the model prevented
options.B: Weekly uptime of the service that runs the fraud model
options.C: Weekly drift in refund claims from the model's training data
options.D: Number of refund holds that reviews overturned in each quarter

questions.key_concept: A KRI must warn before tolerance breaks; when AI errors surface late, input drift from the training data can serve as a leading indicator.
questions.pre_read: Note how long it takes to learn a hold was wrong, then ask which measure moves earlier.
questions.correct_explanation: Wrongful holds are confirmed only after two-month reviews, so a KRI built on them warns after businesses have waited. Drift in refund claims away from the model's training data moves first, signaling that errors may be rising, so management can act before the tolerance breaks; overturned holds later confirm it. Option D, overturned holds, is the runner-up: it measures the right harm, but too late to warn.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because it shows the model's value. But fraud prevented is a performance indicator; it can rise while wrongful holds climb.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because uptime is easy to track. But availability says nothing about whether the model is holding the wrong refunds.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it counts wrongful holds directly. But reviews take two months, so the indicator reports a breach after businesses have already waited for their money.

tips: Eliminate: B tracks availability, which says nothing about wrong holds, and A is a key performance indicator (KPI) of value, not a risk indicator.
Final two: C beats D because drift warns before errors are confirmed; overturned holds measure the harm itself but arrive two months late.
Exam cue: when an AI's errors are confirmed late, pair lagging measures with a leading KRI, such as input drift, that warns before tolerance breaks.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. A claims model's error limit
questions.question: A Brazilian dental-plan provider's data scientists set the maximum wrongful-denial rate for its claims model at 6%, the best rate their models achieved. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have senior management set a tolerance within the risk appetite
options.B: Have the data scientists tighten the limit to 3% and retrain
options.C: Have the IS auditor set the limit from industry benchmarks
options.D: Have the model owner adopt 6% as the claims model's use-level limit

questions.key_concept: AI tolerances express acceptable harm, set by senior management within the board's risk appetite; they are never derived from what a model happens to achieve.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the 6% came from, and who should decide how many wrongful denials are acceptable.
questions.correct_explanation: A tolerance states how much harm the organization will accept, so senior management sets it within the risk appetite the board approved, instead of deriving it from what the model can do. Setting it at the best rate achieved turns the model's limits into the organization's appetite. Having the model owner adopt 6%, option D, is the runner-up: owners do set use-level limits, but inside a tolerance management has set, not from a capability figure.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a stricter limit sounds safer. But the builders would still be setting the limit; they measure against tolerances, they do not decide them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the IS auditor is independent. But setting the limit would mean deciding risk that management owns, which the IS auditor must later assess.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because model owners set use-level limits. But they set them inside a tolerance senior management has approved; adopting 6% still starts from what the model achieved.

tips: Eliminate: B leaves the limit with the builders, who should measure against it, and C has the IS auditor setting a limit it must later assess.
Final two: A beats D because an owner's use-level limit must sit inside a tolerance senior management has set; adopting 6% still starts from capability.
Exam cue: a tolerance set to what the model achieves is backwards; tolerances come from appetite, and the model must meet them.

questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Shared foundation models
questions.question: A Canadian workers' compensation board finds its claims-review, call-center and fraud-detection vendors, which its continuity plan treats as independent, all use a single hosted language model. Which risk should the IS auditor consider MOST significant?

options.A: The vendors' controls reports may not cover the shared model provider
options.B: One provider's outage or update could disrupt three services at once
options.C: Staff may need training on three different vendor interfaces
options.D: The three vendors may give different answers about the same claim

questions.key_concept: AI supply chains run below the direct vendor; several vendors built on one model concentrate failure and change risk in a single provider.
questions.pre_read: Look past the three vendor names and ask what they have in common.
questions.correct_explanation: Three vendors that the continuity plan treats as independent share one dependency. An outage, a withdrawn model version or a silent behavior change at the provider would hit claims review, the call center and fraud detection together, so a plan that assumes one vendor fails at a time would not hold. Controls-report coverage, option A, is the runner-up: it is a real assurance gap, but the concentration exists whatever the reports cover.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because fourth parties often fall outside vendor reports. But better reports would not remove the single point of failure shared by all three services.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because three interfaces add effort. But training cost does not threaten the services the way a shared failure would.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because inconsistent answers confuse injured workers. But inconsistency is a quality issue; a shared provider failing would stop all three services at once.

tips: Eliminate: D is a consistency issue, not a threat to the services, and C is a training cost that does not threaten them either.
Final two: B beats A because a shared model is a single point of failure across three services; better assurance reports would not remove it.
Exam cue: map AI supply chains below the direct vendor; several vendors on one model concentrate risk that contracts with each vendor do not show.
