questions.subtopic: 1C AI risk management. Monitoring a vendor's model
questions.question: A Turkish elevator-maintenance firm licenses a vendor's breakdown-prediction model; its only monitoring is a quarterly accuracy report the vendor itself computes, pooled across all clients. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have the owner compare predictions with recorded breakdowns
options.B: Adopt the vendor's newest model version as soon as it ships
options.C: Have the vendor compute results for the firm's own elevators
options.D: Require the vendor to disclose the model's training data sources

questions.key_concept: Buying AI does not transfer accountability; the buyer monitors a vendor's model in its own setting, independently of vendor-produced reports.
questions.pre_read: Ask who produced the monitoring evidence and whose elevators it describes.
questions.correct_explanation: The vendor's report pools results across all clients, so it cannot show how the model performs on this firm's elevators, and the vendor chooses what to measure. Comparing predictions with technicians' recorded breakdowns gives the owner independent evidence from its own setting. A firm-specific vendor report, option C, is the runner-up: it removes the pooling, but the vendor still computes the measure, so the evidence is not independent.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because newer versions often perform better. But adopting versions untested in the firm's setting adds change risk and does nothing to monitor results.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because results for the firm's own elevators are more relevant. But the vendor still chooses the data and measures, so the evidence stays vendor-controlled.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because training-data transparency helps judge a model. But a description of past data does not show how the model performs on this firm's elevators now.

tips: Eliminate: D describes the model's past training data, not its current results, and B adopts new versions without testing them in the firm's setting.
Final two: A beats C because the owner's own comparison is independent of the vendor; a tailored vendor report is more relevant but still the vendor's measure.
Exam cue: vendor reports on a model are inputs; expect the buyer to monitor the model's results in its own setting, independently of the vendor.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Shared model features
questions.question: A Peruvian store group's marketing team redefined a shared 'loyal customer' feature for its model without telling anyone; the group's credit-limit and fraud models also use it. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have each model team keep its own private copy of the feature
options.B: Have the credit and fraud teams retrain on the new definition
options.C: Have IT limit who can read data in the shared feature store
options.D: Have a named owner approve changes to the shared feature

questions.key_concept: Shared features are data many models depend on; they need a named owner who approves changes and lineage showing which models use them.
questions.pre_read: Trace who else depends on the feature before judging how changes to it should be handled.
questions.correct_explanation: A feature shared by three models is data they all depend on. Redefining it for one model silently changed what the credit-limit and fraud models score, with nobody accountable for the change. A named owner who approves changes, with lineage showing which models use the feature, lets every affected owner assess a change first. Option A, private copies, is the runner-up: they isolate teams, but leave definitions drifting apart unowned.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because separate copies stop one team's change reaching others. But definitions then drift apart with no owner or lineage, and nobody knows which version each model scores.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the models should match the current definition. But that accepts a change nobody assessed for credit or fraud decisions.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because access control protects data. But the problem is who may redefine the feature, not who may read it.

tips: Eliminate: B accepts a change no one assessed for credit or fraud, and C limits who reads the data, not who may redefine it.
Final two: D beats A because an owner who approves changes, with lineage to every model using the feature, lets each model owner assess a change first; private copies drift apart unowned.
Exam cue: shared model inputs need a named owner and lineage to every model that uses them, so one team's change cannot silently alter another's model.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Licensed training data
questions.question: A Dubai property portal's valuation model was trained on a licensed sales-transactions dataset, and the license ends next month. What should the IS auditor consider MOST important to confirm?

options.A: Whether valuations stay accurate once the dataset is deleted
options.B: Whether the license lets the portal keep its published valuations
options.C: Whether the license lets the portal keep using models trained on it
options.D: Whether the dataset was kept encrypted during the license term

questions.key_concept: A trained model keeps what it learned, so data licenses must permit continued use of models trained on the data, not only its storage.
questions.pre_read: Ask what remains of the dataset inside the model after every copy of the data is gone.
questions.correct_explanation: A trained model carries what it learned from the data, so deleting the dataset does not end the portal's use of that data. Whether models trained on licensed data may stay in use after the license ends depends on the license terms; if they forbid it, the model must be retired or retrained. Keeping published valuations, option B, is the runner-up: it is a real license question, but the model keeps producing new valuations daily.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because data loss can affect models. But a model that is already trained does not change when its source data is deleted.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because published valuations were derived from the data. But they are past outputs; the larger exposure is the model, which keeps producing new valuations from what it learned.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because licensed data needs protection. But encryption during the term says nothing about whether use may continue after it ends.

tips: Eliminate: D concerns security during the license, not the right to keep using the data, and A assumes deleting the dataset changes a model already trained.
Final two: C beats B because the model keeps using what it learned to value new listings daily; published valuations are past outputs, a smaller exposure.
Exam cue: rights to use data for training must cover the trained model's life, not just how long the dataset is stored.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Synthetic data from real records
questions.question: A Greek cancer registry plans to share synthetic patient records, produced by a generative model trained on its real records, with outside researchers as non-personal data. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Have researchers sign agreements to keep the synthetic records secure
options.B: Test the synthetic records for close matches to real patients
options.C: Encrypt the synthetic records before sending them to researchers
options.D: Strip names and ID numbers from the real records before generating

questions.key_concept: Synthetic data from a generative model trained on personal records can reproduce real people, so it is tested before being treated as non-personal.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the generative model learned from, and whether its output could still describe a real patient.
questions.correct_explanation: A generative model trained on real records can memorize and reproduce them, especially rare cases, so synthetic output is not automatically non-personal. Testing the synthetic records for near copies of real patients shows whether sharing them could identify anyone. Stripping names first, option D, is the runner-up: it removes direct identifiers, but a rare diagnosis with an age and a town can still identify a patient.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because agreements bind researchers. But a contract does not settle whether the records identify patients; that needs testing first.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because health data needs protection in transit. But encryption protects records on the way, not whether they describe real people.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because removing direct identifiers is standard de-identification. But the records are already generated, and rare combinations of diagnosis, age and place remain for the model to reproduce.

tips: Eliminate: C protects records in transit, not whether they describe real people, and A binds researchers without settling whether the data is personal.
Final two: B beats D because removing names leaves rare combinations a model can reproduce; only testing the output shows whether real patients appear.
Exam cue: synthetic data from a model trained on personal data stays a privacy question until tests show it does not reproduce real people.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Access requests and model scores
questions.question: A Polish ferry operator answers passengers' data-access requests with their bookings and contact details; its pricing model also scores each passenger's likely willingness to pay. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: Passengers are not shown the scores the model infers about them
options.B: Some willingness-to-pay scores may be wrong for individual passengers
options.C: The booking site may not encrypt passengers' card payment details
options.D: Booking history may not be pseudonymized before the model scores it

questions.key_concept: Model inferences, such as scores and profiles, are personal data; privacy duties like access requests must cover them, not only collected records.
questions.pre_read: Ask what information about each passenger exists after the model runs, and whether the response covers it.
questions.correct_explanation: A score the model infers about a passenger is personal data, just like the bookings it was built from. Answering access requests with collected data alone hides the profile the model builds about each person. Pseudonymizing booking history, option D, is the runner-up: it is good privacy by design, but the model would still create a score about each identifiable passenger, and access responses would still leave it out.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because wrong scores can mistreat passengers. But accuracy is a separate question; even a correct score is personal data that access responses should cover.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because payment data is sensitive. But card security is unrelated to what the model creates about each passenger.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because pseudonymization is privacy by design. But the model would still create a score about each identifiable passenger, and access responses would still leave it out.

tips: Eliminate: C is a payment-security issue unrelated to the model, and B concerns whether scores are right, while even a correct score is personal data.
Final two: A beats D because pseudonymized inputs still yield a score about each passenger; inferred scores are personal data that access responses must include.
Exam cue: follow personal data out of the model as well as in; inferred scores and profiles are personal data, not just the records collected.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Copies inside AI indexes
questions.question: An Albanian farm-subsidy agency deletes farmers' applications when their two-year appeal period ends, but its staff assistant answers from a search index built from those applications. What should concern the IS auditor MOST?

options.A: The assistant's answers may weaken once source applications are deleted
options.B: The two-year period may be too short for farmers' appeals
options.C: Indexed text from applications may outlive the deletion of the originals
options.D: Staff may search the index for farmers' details without a business need

questions.key_concept: Retrieval indexes and embeddings hold copies of source text, so deletion and retention schedules must cover them, not only the original records.
questions.pre_read: List every place the applications' text now lives, not just where the originals are stored.
questions.correct_explanation: Deleting the applications removes the originals, but the search index holds chunks of their text, so farmers' personal details stay retrievable after the retention period ends, and the assistant can still quote them. Retention and deletion must reach every AI copy, including indexes and embeddings. Unneeded staff searches, option D, is the runner-up: access limits reduce misuse, but data that should be gone would still be kept.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because deleting sources sounds like it would starve the assistant. But the index keeps its own copies, so answers continue, and that is the problem.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because retention should match appeal periods. But the agency already keeps applications for the full appeal period; the gap is copies kept after it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because personal data needs access limits. But tighter access would still leave farmers' details stored past their deletion date.

tips: Eliminate: B questions an appeal period that retention already matches, and A expects answers to weaken, though the index keeps its own copies.
Final two: C beats D because access limits control who sees the data but not how long it is kept; the index holds farmers' details past their deletion date.
Exam cue: deleting source records does not delete their copies inside AI indexes, embeddings or caches; retention schedules must reach every copy.

questions.subtopic: 1D Privacy and data governance. Retiring fine-tuned models
questions.question: A Lebanese bank retired a chatbot fine-tuned on customer chats and deleted the chat training set, but the fine-tuned model files remain on a shared research drive. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Encrypt the shared research drive that stores the model files
options.B: Confirm that the chat training set was securely deleted from every system
options.C: Keep the model files for reuse in the bank's next chatbot
options.D: Handle the model files under the same rules as the customer chats

questions.key_concept: A model fine-tuned on personal data may memorize it, so retiring the system means disposing of or restricting the model files, not only the data.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model files contain after training, not just what was deleted.
questions.correct_explanation: A model fine-tuned on customer chats can memorize and reproduce them, so its files can hold the same personal data as the deleted training set. Leaving them on a shared drive undoes the deletion; they need the same disposal or access rules as the chats. Confirming the training set's deletion, option B, is the runner-up: it checks the source data, but the model files still carry what was learned from it.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because encryption protects stored files. But staff with drive access could still load the model and draw out memorized chat details.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because complete deletion of source data is a sound check. But the model files still carry what the model memorized from those chats.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because reuse saves building costs. But reuse would carry memorized customer chats into a new system without a fresh basis.

tips: Eliminate: C would carry memorized chats into a new chatbot, and A protects the drive from outsiders but not from staff who can load and query the model.
Final two: D beats B because deleting the training set leaves what the model memorized; the model files need the same rules as the chats.
Exam cue: when an AI system is retired, dispose of trained models like the personal data they learned from, while keeping records needed to explain past decisions.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Testing a fairness criterion
questions.question: A French broadband provider's fairness criterion covers ethnic groups, but privacy rules bar collecting ethnicity, so its purchased credit-check model has never been tested against it. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Treat the model as fair since ethnicity is not among its inputs
options.B: Have the owners agree a lawful way to test outcomes across groups
options.C: Rely on the vendor's fairness audit, which covered ethnic groups
options.D: Have the data team infer ethnicity from names to test fairness

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI characteristics can conflict; owners decide and document how to test fairness within privacy limits, since omitting an input does not prove fairness.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each option keeps both fairness and privacy in play, or gives one of them up.
questions.correct_explanation: Fairness and privacy are both trustworthy-AI characteristics, and here they pull against each other. The model owners must decide, and record, how fairness will be tested within the privacy rules, for example through a lawful, protected study approved with the data protection officer. The vendor's fairness audit, option C, is the runner-up: it covered ethnic groups, but on the vendor's test data, not outcomes for this provider's customers.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the model cannot use what it never sees. But inputs such as postcode or employment history can act as proxies, so outcomes can still differ by group.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the audit covered ethnic groups. But it tested the vendor's data, not this provider's customers, and leaves the conflict between fairness and privacy unresolved here.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it gives group labels to test with. But guessing ethnicity from names creates sensitive data the rules bar, and the guesses are often wrong.

tips: Eliminate: A treats leaving ethnicity out of the inputs as proof of fairness, though proxies remain, and D creates, by guessing, the sensitive data the privacy rules bar.
Final two: B beats C because a vendor's audit covers its own test data, not this provider's customers; the owners must still find a lawful way to test fairness here.
Exam cue: when two trustworthy-AI characteristics conflict, expect owners to decide and document the balance, not drop one of them.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 Section 3.7 (Fair with Harmful Bias Managed); NIST AI 100-1 MEASURE 2.11 (Fairness and bias evaluated and documented)

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Criteria for a companion chatbot
questions.question: A Hong Kong charity's companion chatbot talks with older residents living alone, and some report feeling unwell; the owner's criteria cover accuracy and response time. Which added criterion should the IS auditor consider MOST important?

options.A: Seeded distress messages reach a staff member within minutes
options.B: The chatbot is retested against the criteria after every model update
options.C: Residents are told plainly whenever they are talking to AI
options.D: Replies arrive within two seconds even at peak evening hours

questions.key_concept: Trustworthy-AI criteria should cover the characteristic most at stake for the people affected; for vulnerable users, safety needs tested escalation.
questions.pre_read: Picture the worst message a resident living alone might send, and ask which criterion would catch it.
questions.correct_explanation: Some residents already report feeling unwell to the chatbot, and for people living alone a missed message about a fall or a crisis could cause serious harm. Safety means the system fails safely, and tests with seeded distress messages show whether a person is alerted in time. Telling residents plainly when they talk to AI, option C, is the runner-up: transparency matters, but a missed emergency would harm residents far more.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because model updates can change behavior. But retesting only reruns the existing criteria, which contain no test of how emergencies are handled.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because older residents should know they are talking to AI. But transparency adds less protection than catching an emergency that a resident living alone reports.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because quick replies help residents. But response time is already among the owner's criteria, and speed alone does not get help to someone in crisis.

tips: Eliminate: D repeats response time, which the owner's criteria already cover, and B reruns those same criteria, which still contain no test for emergencies.
Final two: A beats C because a missed distress message could seriously harm someone living alone; transparency matters, but the safety gap carries the greater harm.
Exam cue: match criteria to the characteristic most at stake for the people affected; for vulnerable users, test how the system handles emergencies.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. New uses under AI laws
questions.question: A Spanish hotel chain's assistant, rated minimal risk under a risk-based AI law when it only summarized résumés, now ranks candidates for interviews. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Buy a compliance tool that checks the assistant against AI laws
options.B: Have legal counsel reassess its risk class for the new ranking use
options.C: Keep the earlier rating, since the underlying model has not changed
options.D: Have HR test the rankings for bias against groups of candidates

questions.key_concept: Risk-based AI laws classify systems by intended use, so a new use of an unchanged model can bring a higher risk class and new duties.
questions.pre_read: Compare what the assistant does now with what it did when it was classified.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based AI laws classify by intended use, not by technology. Ranking job candidates is a use such laws often treat as high risk, so the earlier minimal-risk rating may no longer hold, and duties such as oversight, documentation and logging could now apply. Counsel must reassess before controls are mapped. Bias testing, option D, is the runner-up: it is a sound control, but which obligations it must meet is not yet settled.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because tools track many laws. But a tool cannot make the legal judgment on applicability; governance comes before tooling.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the technology is the same. But risk-based laws classify by use; ranking candidates is a different use from summarizing résumés.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because ranking candidates raises fairness risk. But bias testing comes after counsel settles which duties apply, so the right controls can be mapped to them.

tips: Eliminate: C ties the risk class to the model, though such laws classify by use, and A buys a tool before anyone has decided which duties apply.
Final two: B beats D because the new use may carry new legal duties; bias testing is sound, but which obligations apply must be settled first.
Exam cue: under risk-based AI laws, a new use of the same model can change its risk class; reassess applicability before mapping controls.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 GOVERN 1.1 (Legal and regulatory requirements involving AI are understood and managed); NIST AI 100-1 MAP 1.4 (Business value or context of use defined or re-evaluated)

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Evidence of AI compliance
questions.question: A Czech agricultural-drone maker's compliance tool has a language model read its policies and mark each applicable AI duty as met. Which evidence would BEST support the IS auditor's conclusion on compliance?

options.A: A board resolution adopting the tool as the compliance standard
options.B: A second language model confirming every duty marked met
options.C: Each duty traced to an owned control shown to be operating
options.D: The policy passages the model cited for each duty marked met

questions.key_concept: AI compliance is shown by mapping each applicable duty to an owned, operating control; a model's compliance marks, even with citations, are leads.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the model looked at to mark each duty, and whether that shows a control operates.
questions.correct_explanation: A language model's 'met' marks are leads: it judged from policies, which show what is intended, not what operates. Compliance is shown only when each duty maps to a control with an owner and evidence that it operates, such as decision logs the drones keep or tested pilot overrides. The cited policy passages, option D, are the runner-up: they let the marks be checked, but only against documents, not operation.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because board adoption shows commitment. But a resolution adopting a tool shows no control operates for any duty.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a second source's agreement looks like corroboration. But a second model reads the same policies, so it confirms intent, not operation, and may share the first model's errors.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because cited passages make the model's marks look grounded. But policies show what is intended; only owned controls with evidence show a duty is met.

tips: Eliminate: A adopts the tool by resolution, which shows no control works, and B has a second model re-read the same policies, which still shows only intent.
Final two: C beats D because the model judged from policies, which show intent; compliance is shown by owned controls with evidence that they operate.
Exam cue: an AI tool's compliance marks are leads; test the chain of duty, control, owner and operating evidence behind each one.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Frameworks for generative AI
questions.question: A Norwegian patent office follows the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, yet its filing-summary assistant's risk assessment lists only accuracy and drift. Which source should the IS auditor recommend as BEST for widening it?

options.A: The vendor's model card listing the model's benchmark test results
options.B: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework used as the security baseline
options.C: The EU AI Act's list of banned AI practices
options.D: The twelve risks set out in NIST AI 600-1

questions.key_concept: The NIST Generative AI Profile extends the AI RMF to generative AI risks, such as confabulation and information integrity, that predictive-style assessments miss.
questions.pre_read: Ask which risks a summarizing assistant has that a forecasting model would not.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI 600-1 Generative AI Profile applies the AI RMF to generative AI and describes risks a predictive-style assessment misses, such as confabulation, information integrity and intellectual property, all relevant to summaries of patent filings. The vendor's model card, option A, is the runner-up: it describes the model's tested limits, but in general terms, not the risks of this use.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because model cards list known limits. But they describe the vendor's model in general, not the risks of summarizing patent filings for this office.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because NIST frameworks work together. But the Cybersecurity Framework organizes security outcomes, not risks such as invented facts in summaries.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because AI law sets firm limits. But banned practices mark uses that are prohibited outright; they do not list the risks of a lawful summarizing assistant.

tips: Eliminate: C lists banned practices, not the risks of a lawful assistant, and B organizes cybersecurity outcomes, not risks such as invented facts.
Final two: D beats A because the profile sets out generative AI risks to map against this use; a model card describes the vendor's model in general.
Exam cue: for generative AI, widen risk work with the NIST Generative AI Profile; risks such as confabulation fall outside predictive-model checks.

questions.subtopic: 1E Ethics, regulations and standards. Framework claims by vendors
questions.question: A Philippine university is choosing a vendor's model that flags essays as AI-written; the vendor says the model is 'NIST AI RMF certified' and unbiased. What should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Request bias test results for this model on similar essays
options.B: Have the vendor sign a formal statement that the model is unbiased
options.C: Ask which accredited body issued the vendor's NIST AI RMF certificate
options.D: Accept the claim, since NIST frameworks set recognized requirements

questions.key_concept: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance with no NIST certification; framework 'certified' claims are assertions, and model claims need model-level tests.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the framework named in the claim can certify anything at all.
questions.correct_explanation: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, and NIST offers no certification against it, so 'NIST AI RMF certified' is the vendor's own description and says nothing about this model's fairness. Bias test results for this model, on essays like the university's, answer the claim. Asking which body issued the certificate, option C, is the runner-up: it is normal due diligence, but there is no recognized scheme to check.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it puts the vendor on record. But a signed statement is still the vendor's assertion, not evidence from testing.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because checking a certificate's issuer is normal due diligence. But NIST offers no certification against the voluntary AI RMF, so any 'certificate' is a private opinion.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because NIST publications are respected. But the AI RMF is voluntary and use-case agnostic; it sets no pass mark a model can be certified against.

tips: Eliminate: D accepts a claim because NIST is respected, and B swaps evidence for the vendor's own signed assertion.
Final two: A beats C because NIST offers no certification against the AI RMF, so there is no issuer to check; only this model's test results answer the bias claim.
Exam cue: a voluntary framework guides risk work but certifies nothing; meet any 'certified' claim about a model with that model's own test results.
